title: Six Lots, and Joshua's Own Town
summary: The remaining six lots are drawn at Shiloh. Simeon receives towns within Judah's large territory; Zebulun, Issachar, Asher, and Naphtali receive the lands of Galilee and the north; and Dan receives land near the coast, though a later note records that the Danites lost it and moved north to capture Leshem. Last of all, the Israelites give Joshua the town he asks for, Timnath-serah in Ephraim, and the division of the land is complete.
story: Chapter 18 began the lots at Shiloh with Benjamin; chapter 19 finishes them. The chapter moves quickly through six tribes, with borders for some and only town lists for others. It closes the long section on the allotment that began in chapter 13 with two fitting endings. The leader who had divided the land for everyone else receives his own portion only after every tribe has theirs, and verse 51 formally seals the whole process at the Tent of Meeting. Chapters 20 and 21 will then add the special cities, the cities of refuge and the towns of the Levites, before the book turns to its farewells.
historical:
The northern tribes received the region later called Galilee, with the Jezreel Valley, the hills around Mount Tabor, and the land west and north of the Sea of Galilee (here Chinnereth). Many towns appear later in the story. Gath-hepher in Zebulun was the hometown of the prophet Jonah (2 Kings 14:25). Shunem in Issachar was where Elisha was hosted by a Shunammite woman (2 Kings 4), and Jezreel became a royal residence of Ahab's dynasty. Cabul in Asher gave its name to the district of towns Solomon handed to Hiram of Tyre (1 Kings 9:13). Kedesh and Hazor in Naphtali reappear in chapter 20 and in the time of Deborah. The Bethlehem of verse 15 is a town in Zebulun, not the Bethlehem of Judah.

Simeon's towns in the far south match a parallel list in 1 Chronicles 4:28-33. Sharuhen is known from Egyptian records as a stronghold besieged by the pharaoh Ahmose in the sixteenth century BC. Dan's original land, near Joppa on the coast, lay beside the Philistines. Judges 18 tells how the Danites, pressed out of it, migrated north and took Laish (Leshem), renaming it Dan. Excavations at Tel Dan in the 1990s found an Aramaic inscription from the ninth century BC that refers to the house of David, one of the earliest mentions of David outside the Bible.
cultural:
Simeon's lack of a separate territory fulfills the words of Jacob's blessing, which said that Simeon and Levi would be scattered in Israel because of their violence at Shechem (Genesis 49:5-7; Genesis 34). Levi was scattered through priestly towns; Simeon was absorbed into Judah, and later lists hardly treat it as a distinct tribe. Asher's allotment reached toward Tyre and Sidon, but the Phoenician coastal cities were never actually taken (Judges 1:31-32), and Asher lived among the Canaanites there.

Joshua's receiving a town at his own request, after all the tribes had theirs, reflects the ideal of a leader who serves the people before himself. Rebuilding a town meant fortifying it and restoring its houses so a family could live and farm there. Judges 2:9 records that Joshua was buried there, under the name Timnath-heres.
literary: The chapter is built from six parallel units, each opening with a formula like "The second lot came out" and closing with "This was the inheritance of the clans of the tribe of" followed by the tribe's name. The lots are numbered from second to seventh, continuing from Benjamin, the first lot, in chapter 18. Some units give borders and towns (Zebulun, Asher, Naphtali), others mainly towns (Simeon, Issachar, Dan). The parenthesis about Dan in verse 47 looks ahead to later events, a sign that the book was completed after the time of Joshua. Verses 49-51 bring the whole section to a close, forming a frame with 14:1, which named the same three distributing authorities: Eleazar the priest, Joshua, and the heads of the families.

outline.t: Dan, and its later move north
Joshua's inheritance and the end of the division

doctrines.note: Every tribe receives its land by lot at the tabernacle, and even the old words of Jacob's blessing about Simeon come to pass. God's purposes work through centuries and through ordinary processes like casting lots and drawing borders.

Simeon's scattering within Judah recalls the violence at Shechem in Genesis 34. The consequences of a family's sin can reach down generations, even while God continues to give that family a place among his people.
Joshua takes his own inheritance last, after every tribe is provided for. Leadership among God's people is presented as service, not privilege, a pattern that Jesus makes central.

words.note: Goral, lot. Each tribe's portion is introduced by the lot that came out for it. The word emphasizes that the division was God's decision, received at Shiloh before the LORD, not a bargain struck among the strongest tribes.

Paga, to meet, reach, or touch. In the boundary descriptions it is used when a border touches a place or another tribe's land. Elsewhere the same verb can mean to meet someone in order to plead with them, and so to intercede, which shows the word's range, though here it is purely geographical.

Dan, a name linked in Genesis 30:6 with the verb to judge or vindicate. The tribe's story in this chapter is unsettled: it receives land near the coast, loses it, and moves to the far north, where its town of Dan became the northern limit of Israel in the phrase from Dan to Beersheba.

christ: Two threads link this chapter to the story of Jesus. The first is geographical. The lands of Zebulun and Naphtali, allotted here, later became Galilee. Isaiah 9:1-2 promised that this region, humbled by invasion, would see a great light, and Matthew 4:13-16 says that Jesus made his home at Capernaum in the region of Zebulun and Naphtali in fulfillment of that promise. Most of his ministry took place in these tribal lands. The second thread is thematic: Joshua receives his inheritance last, after serving everyone else, and Jesus taught that whoever wants to be great must be the servant of all (Mark 10:43-45), then gave his life for those he led.
questions: Joshua took his own inheritance only after everyone else had theirs. What would it look like for you to put others' needs before your own in a place where you have authority?
Simeon's history shaped its inheritance, yet it still had a place in Israel. How does this give hope to people who carry the consequences of their family's past?
Dan lost its first territory and had to move. How do you respond when a place or role you were given doesn't hold?
